title: By the River
focus: despair and renewal by the river

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha reaches the river sick of himself and comes close to ending his life (By the River, paras. 2–5; referenced, not quoted). From deep within comes the sacred word Om, and he falls into a deep sleep under a coconut tree. He wakes renewed; Govinda, now a monk, has watched over him without recognizing him. Siddhartha reflects that he had to experience despair to learn its emptiness, and decides to stay by the river.

Next, craft. I notice the line is only three words, set alone after the monk's puzzled question, so the smile answers him before any words do. The strongest word is “smiled”: the smile is the first calm, knowing gesture after his despair at the river, so it marks a man who has come back to himself. Then, effect. Why does Siddhartha smile when the monk asks how he knows his name? My answer: The monk is his old friend Govinda, who cannot recognize him; Siddhartha smiles because he has just woken by the river calm and renewed, no longer the weary rich merchant who came to the river in despair.

items.text: What does Siddhartha's despair lead him toward at the river?
items.lookFor: Despair so deep that he wants to die (By the River, paras. 2–5, referenced only)
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Toward a wish to die. Point students to the paragraphs by number only and do not read them aloud: By the River, paragraphs 2–5. Later he names it himself as “the thought of suicide” (By the River, paragraph 42). Teacher note: some schools' guidelines may treat this passage differently.

items.text: What stops him?
items.lookFor: The word Om rising within
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: The word Om, rising from deep in his memory: “It was a word, a syllable, which he, without thinking, with a slurred voice, spoke to himself” (By the River, paragraph 6)… and “when the Om entered his consciousness” (By the River, paragraph 7).

items.text: Why does Govinda doubt that Siddhartha is a pilgrim?
items.lookFor: His rich clothes, fine shoes and perfumed hair
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Because he looks like a rich man: “You’re wearing a rich man’s garments, you’re wearing the shoes of a distinguished gentleman, and your hair, with the fragrance of perfume, is not a pilgrim’s hair” (By the River, paragraph 28).

items.text: Does Govinda recognize him at first?
items.lookFor: No
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: No: “Siddhartha saw that Govinda did not recognise him” (By the River, paragraph 12). Govinda knows him only after he gives his name: “Now, I’m recognising you” (By the River, paragraph 24).

items.text: What does Siddhartha promise himself he will never do again?
items.lookFor: Delude himself into thinking he is wise
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “No, never again I will, as I used to like doing so much, delude myself into thinking that Siddhartha was wise!” (By the River, paragraph 44)

items.text: Retell the three most important events of “By the River” in order, in one sentence each.
items.lookFor: Siddhartha reaches the river sick of himself and comes close to ending his life (By the River, paras. 2–5; referenced, not quoted). From deep within comes the sacred word Om, and he falls into a deep sleep under a coconut tree. He wakes renewed; Govinda, now a monk, has watched over him without recognizing him. Siddhartha reflects that he had to experience despair to learn its emptiness, and decides to stay by the river.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: In despair he comes to the river (paragraph 1; paragraphs 2–5 are cite-only); the word Om stops him and he sleeps under the coconut tree (paragraphs 6–9); he wakes renewed, talks with Govinda and decides to stay by the river (paragraphs 12–49).

items.text: Which characters appear or are mentioned in “By the River”? Name two and one thing each says or does.
items.lookFor: Names and actions taken from the chapter; check against the teacher summary.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Two of: Govinda, who guards the sleeper without knowing him (paragraph 14); Kamala and Kamaswami, remembered as the life he fled (paragraph 45); Gotama, whose teaching Govinda still follows (paragraph 42).

items.text: Where and when does “By the River” take place? Point to the line that tells you.
items.lookFor: A place/time detail quoted from the chapter.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: By the river in the forest, one day and night after he leaves the city: “Siddhartha walked through the forest, was already far from the city” (By the River, paragraph 1)… The coconut tree on the bank is in paragraph 9.

items.text: Reread: “These had been his possession, his power and strength, his solid staff; in the busy, laborious years of his youth, he had learned these three feats, nothing else.” What does “laborious” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: laborious: needing much hard work.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Laborious” here means: needing much hard work. In By the River, paragraph 38, Siddhartha remembers that in his hard-working youth he learned only three feats: fasting, waiting and thinking.

items.text: Reread: “And how could he not have loved everybody and everything in this moment, in the glorious hour after his wonderful sleep, filled with Om!” What does “glorious” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?
items.lookFor: glorious: wonderful; full of splendour.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: “Glorious” here means: wonderful; full of splendour. In By the River, paragraph 37, after his deep sleep Siddhartha wakes into a joyful hour in which he loves everyone and everything.

items.text: What does “By the River” suggest about despair and renewal by the river? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: A stated inference (for example, that renewal comes through despair, not around it) backed by one located line, such as the one in By the River, paragraph 47.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The chapter suggests that renewal comes through despair, not around it. Support: “Was it not due to this death, that he was now like a child, so full of trust, so without fear, so full of joy?” (By the River, paragraph 47)

items.text: Find one example of symbolism in this chapter. What does it reveal that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: Look for objects, places or actions that stand for larger ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The bird in his chest (“that the bird, the joyful source and voice in him was still alive after all” (By the River, paragraph 45)) stands for the inner voice that died in Kamala’s cage; it shows renewal as something that survived inside him.

items.text: How does the imagery in this chapter shape what we understand about despair and renewal by the river?
items.lookFor: Look for sensory details (sight, sound, cold, light) and what mood they create.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Images of sleep and waking (“Never before by sleep, he had been thus refreshed, thus renewed, thus rejuvenated!” (By the River, paragraph 11)) and of the rushing water (paragraph 49) make renewal physical, like a body waking.

items.text: In the passage that begins “For a long time, he pondered his transformation, listened to the bird, as it sang for joy.”, why might Hesse have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Diction analysis of two words in the anchor passage.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: In By the River, paragraph 47, “pondered” shows calm thought instead of panic, and “sang for joy” gives the inner bird its voice back; the words mark how far he has come since the start of the chapter.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “By the River”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: Siddhartha reaches the river sick of himself and comes close to ending his life (By the River, paras. 2–5; referenced, not quoted). From deep within comes the sacred word Om, and he falls into a deep sleep under a coconut tree. He wakes renewed; Govinda, now a monk, has watched over him without recognizing him. Siddhartha reflects that he had to experience…
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The cause is the word Om (By the River, paragraph 7), which wakes him from despair. Effect: after sleep he is “renewed” (paragraph 11) and will stay by the river, where the next chapter finds him.

items.text: How does “By the River” build on “Sansara”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A causal or structural link between this and the previous chapter.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Cause and effect: in “Sansara” he left the city in the night; this chapter begins with that flight and its end, “there was no going back for him” (By the River, paragraph 1).

items.text: What can we infer about a character's motives from what they say and do here, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: An inference about motive supported by a quoted line.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Govinda says he stayed only to guard a sleeper (paragraph 14), but his kindness to a stranger shows the Buddha’s teaching at work; Siddhartha claims he is a pilgrim (paragraph 27) while he really has nowhere to go.

items.text: The bell-ringer asked: “Why does Siddhartha say he had to experience despair himself?” Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer anchored in the text.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A revised answer should use his own explanation: he had to fall to the lowest point to find grace again, as he says in By the River, paragraph 42 (cite by paragraph; the line names suicide, so do not ask students to read it aloud). Teacher note: some schools' guidelines may treat this passage differently.

items.text: Where does theme appear, and how does it connect this chapter to the larger concern with the unity of all things?
items.lookFor: Look for statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: The theme of oneness appears in Om, “the old word which is the beginning and the end of all prayers” (By the River, paragraph 6), and in his wish to forget and then regain “the oneness” (paragraph 42).

items.text: Background: Om is the sacred syllable in Hindu and Buddhist traditions, representing ultimate reality. How does knowing this change the way you read one moment in the chapter?
items.lookFor: A specific moment reread in light of the context.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Knowing that Om stands for ultimate reality explains why one word can stop him (paragraph 7): it reconnects him to everything he had lost, not just to a habit of prayer.

items.text: A critic might argue: “Rebirth by water is a classic archetype; the river becomes the novel's central symbol.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Agree in part: the river becomes the place of renewal (paragraph 49). A text counterpoint: the renewal is caused by Om and sleep (paragraphs 6–11), not by the water itself.

items.text: Which character in this chapter acts most wisely, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: An evaluation using an explicit criterion and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: With kindness as the standard, Govinda is wisest: he guards a stranger (paragraph 14). Siddhartha’s earlier despair is least wise, but he judges it himself in paragraph 42.

items.text: Rewrite one moment of “By the River” from the point of view of a different character. What does the new angle reveal or hide about despair and renewal by the river?
items.lookFor: A rewrite that keeps the chapter’s events accurate, speaks in the chosen character’s voice, and ends with a sentence on what the new angle shows or hides.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Govinda’s view of the meeting (By the River, paragraphs 12–36) works well: he sees a rich man asleep in the forest and doubts his words, which hides the inner rebirth.

items.text: Write three questions of your own about “By the River”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions at three levels, each answerable from the chapter, traded and answered with a line.
followUps: Which of your three questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Example set: recall, ‘Under what tree does he sleep?’ (coconut, paragraph 9); why/how, ‘Why doesn’t Govinda recognise him?’ (paragraph 24); what if, ‘Should Siddhartha have gone with Govinda?’

items.text: Connect this chapter to the river and time: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Hesse need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment of thematic development across the work.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Strong start: the river already seems to have something to tell him (“It seemed to him as if the river had something special to tell him” (By the River, paragraph 49)). Hesse needs to show what the river teaches about time.

items.text: Is the symbolism in this chapter effective, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: An evaluative judgment with criteria and evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Effective: the bird links back to the dead songbird of “Sansara” and returns here alive (paragraph 45). Some readers find the bird stated too directly.

items.text: Compare how “By the River” treats despair and renewal by the river with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Siddhartha see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A comparison should name a story of hitting bottom and starting over and quote “Was it not due to this death, that he was now like a child” (By the River, paragraph 47); Siddhartha’s renewal is quiet and inward.

items.text: Predict what “The Ferryman” will bring, using two clues from this chapter. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction or judgment justified with textual clues.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Clues: the river seems to have something to tell him (paragraph 49) and he decides not to leave it (paragraph 49). Prediction: he will stay by the river and learn from it.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of this chapter (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about despair and renewal by the river?
items.lookFor: A modern setting, characters and conflict that keep the chapter’s core idea, with the one element that must not change named.
followUps: Which line from the chapter does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: A modern version keeps someone at the end of their rope who is stopped by a sudden memory of something sacred and wakes renewed. What must stay is the turn caused by Om (paragraph 7). Avoid depicting method.

items.text: What question would you most like to ask Hermann Hesse about this chapter, and what answer do you think the text itself gives?
items.lookFor: A student-generated question answered from evidence.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Example: ‘Why does one word change everything?’ The text answers in paragraph 7: Om brings back what all his recent agony had not.

contentNotes.teacherNote: At the river Siddhartha despairs and comes close to ending his life. Those lines (By the River, paras. 2–5) stay complete in the book text but are referred to by paragraph only; no lesson item quotes them or asks about a method. Keep the focus on the turn: “And in the moment when the sound of Om touched Siddhartha’s ear, his dormant spirit suddenly woke up and realized the foolishness of his actions.” (Hesse, 1922/2015, By the River, para. 6) No one in the novel dies by suicide: Kamala dies of a snakebite (The Ferryman, paras. 47–64), and Siddhartha is stopped by the word Om (By the River, para. 6). Teacher note: some schools' guidelines may treat this passage differently.
